title: Nothing to envy
hook: keep death and exile before your eyes daily, and you won't grasp or envy (Enchiridion 21)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was the insult, completed by your own judgment. Your line was a breath before.

Two words sit at the start of section twenty-one, and neither is cheerful: death and exile. It's a strange place to look for a cure for envy. Envy looks sideways, at a neighbor's new kitchen, a friend's easy promotion, the couple whose photos never seem to have a bad day. Epictetus points somewhere else entirely, and he asks for it every day, not once in a while. The note in the handbook is short and blunt, and the payoff he promises is an odd one.
screen: `DEATH AND EXILE.` → `ENVY LOOKS SIDEWAYS.` → `EVERY DAY, NOT ONCE IN A WHILE.`

segments.voice: Let death and exile, and everything that seems terrible, be before your eyes every day, Epictetus says, and death most of all. Then, he says, you'll never think anything low or petty, and you'll never want anything too much. Notice what he doesn't promise. Not that you'll be less afraid, or more cheerful. He promises a change in what you want. Here's how it works. Envy depends on a sense that the thing you envy is huge. Their promotion, their renovation, their perfect vacation. Set it in the light of death and it shrinks to its real size, not worthless, just the size of something that will be left behind. The Stoics weren't alone here. In Plato's Phaedo, Socrates calls philosophy a kind of practice for dying. The Latin phrase memento mori, remember you'll die, names the same habit. And the gentle part. This isn't meant to darken the day. Done gently, it can work the other way. The coffee tastes like coffee. The annoying coworker becomes a person who will also die, which is strangely tender. And envy, that tight, sour feeling, loosens, because in this light there's nothing to win. Everyone at the table, the one with the new car and the one with the old bike, is on the same short visit. If death feels too heavy today, start with exile: picture leaving behind everything you own. It does the same quiet work.
screen: `DEATH AND EXILE, BEFORE YOUR EYES.` · `NOTHING PETTY, NOTHING TOO MUCH.` · `ENVY SHRINKS TO ITS REAL SIZE.` · `THE SAME SHORT VISIT.` · then, large: `NOTHING TO ENVY.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you envy, someone's house, job, body or ease, and gently widen the picture: fifty years from now, or a hundred, the house belongs to strangers, the job is a line in a story nobody tells, the person is gone, and so are you. Hold it without fear, the way you'd look at the sea. Then look back at the thing you envied, and see what size it is now.
Memento mori. Latin for remember you'll die; Epictetus' daily habit: keep death and exile before your eyes, and you'll want nothing too much. Today's word.
Your line: on the same short visit. In that light, there's nothing to win. That's day three hundred fifty-three.

howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners briefly bring death or loss to mind each day, as a way of loosening envy and grasping rather than as a source of fear.
